work.headingAccent: From a URL you paste to a report you can forward to your investor.
work.s1Desc: We fetch what your users already download: the page and its scripts. We look for keys, open databases, missing auth, absent headers. We store nothing, and we mean that literally: no database, no log of your URL.
work.s2Title: You get a score and the top three
work.s2Desc: Not a list of 200 lint warnings. The three findings that could end you this week, in the order we would fix them, and if we found a key we show it to you with the secret redacted.
work.s3Desc: Now we go inside. Auth, database rules, the payment path, rate limits, secrets, dependencies, the things a scan from outside cannot see.
work.s4Tag: sorted by which AI tool caused it
work.s4Desc: Every finding graded critical, major or minor. Mapped to the OWASP Top 10. An hour estimate per fix. And categorized by the tool that produced it, so you can see what Lovable did to you and what Cursor did.
work.s5Desc: The report is written so any competent engineer can implement it. If you want us to do the work, we quote it after the audit, never before, because a fixed price for a fix on code we have not read is a number somebody made up.
work.s6Title: If we fix it, you get tests
work.s6Tag: and something you can hand over
work.s6Desc: A deployment, tests, and a codebase a real engineer can take on. The point is not that you need us forever. The point is that you can stop being the only person who knows how it works.

faq.subtitle: AI got you eighty percent of the way. The last twenty is a different job.
faq.q1: My app works and nobody has complained. Why do I need <brand></brand>?
faq.a1: Because the failure mode here is silent. Nobody complains about a database that anyone can read, they just read it. A scan of over 1,430 apps built with Lovable found 5,711 vulnerabilities: 85% were missing row-level security, 62% had API keys sitting in the browser bundle, 45% could be logged into without a password. Your app working is not evidence that it is closed. It is evidence that nobody has looked yet.
faq.q2: What exactly do you check? Give me the list.
faq.a2: The free scan looks at what your users already download: secrets in the client bundle, a Supabase or Firebase key with too much power, missing security headers, an exposed environment file. The paid audit goes inside: authentication and authorisation, row-level security, the payment path, rate limits, input validation, dependency vulnerabilities, secrets handling, backups, and whether anything in your logs contains personal data.
faq.q3: Do I have to give you my code or my database password?
faq.a3: Not for the scan. It reads only what is already public, which is the uncomfortable point. For the audit we need read access to the repository, and we will sign whatever your lawyer wants first. We never need a production database password and you should be suspicious of anyone who asks for one.
faq.q4: Will you break my app while fixing it?
faq.a4: We work on a branch, we write tests before we change anything that matters, and you approve the deployment. But we are also going to be honest: closing a database that was open changes behaviour, and if some part of your app was quietly relying on that hole, it will stop working. We would rather it stop working in staging than continue working for a stranger.
faq.q5: Can you fix it, or do you have to rebuild it?
faq.a5: Usually fix. A rebuild is what a shop recommends when it wants a bigger invoice, and most vibe-coded apps have good bones and terrible edges: the product logic is fine, the auth and the data rules and the money path are not. If a rebuild really is the answer we will tell you, with the reasons, and you should get a second opinion anyway.
faq.q6: How much is the audit and how much is the fix?
faq.a6: The audit is 2,500 dollars, fixed, five business days. The fix is quoted afterwards, and we will not quote it before, because a fixed price on code nobody has read is a number invented to win a deal. If the audit finds nothing above minor severity, you pay nothing at all.
faq.q7: What if the audit finds nothing serious?
faq.a7: Then you pay nothing, and you get the report anyway, and you can hand it to an investor as evidence. We can promise that because the published data says it will almost never happen. If your app is the exception, we would genuinely like to see it.
faq.a8: The scan is about a minute. The audit is five business days from the moment we have access. A fix depends on what we find, and the report gives an hour estimate per finding so you can decide before you commit to anything.
faq.q9: Can my own developer implement your fixes instead of you?
faq.a9: Yes, and the report is deliberately written so he can. It has the file, the line, the severity, the OWASP category, the fix, and the hours. We would rather you fixed it with someone you trust than not fixed it because we were expensive.
faq.q10: I built it in Lovable. Do I have to leave the platform?
faq.a10: Not necessarily. A lot of what is wrong can be fixed inside it: the database rules, the auth, the paywall, the keys. What you cannot do inside it is version control, tests, and a deployment story, and at some point you will want those. We will tell you honestly where that line is for your app rather than pushing you off the platform to sell you a migration.
faq.q11: Will I be able to keep prompting after you are done?
faq.a11: Yes, and this is the part most rescue shops quietly do not want. We will leave you a codebase that an AI tool can still work in, with the dangerous parts fenced off and tests around them, so the next prompt cannot silently reopen the hole we just closed.
faq.q12: What happens to my data during the audit? Do you sign an NDA?
faq.a12: We sign the NDA before we look at anything. During the audit we work against a copy where we can, we never pull production personal data, and when it is over we destroy our access. The free scan stores nothing at all: not your URL, not the finding, not an email.
faq.q13: My investor wants technical due diligence. Can I use your report?
faq.a13: That is what most people use it for, and it is the reason it is a document rather than a dashboard. It says what was checked, what was found, what was fixed, and what remains. An honest report with three open items reads better to a serious investor than a clean one nobody believes.
faq.q14: I have paying users right now. What do I do TODAY?
faq.a14: Run the scan, it costs nothing and takes a minute. If it finds a service-role key or an open table, rotate the key immediately, before you talk to us or anyone else. We would rather you fixed the worst of it yourself in the next hour than waited a week for a proposal.

paywall.eyebrow: Twenty seconds, in your own browser
paywall.heading: This is how they got past your paywall.
paywall.subtitle: 27% of monetized apps in the scan gate a paid feature in the browser. Here is what that means, done to a fake app, in front of you.
paywall.doIt: Do what a user did in 2025
paywall.explain: The check was in the browser, so it belongs to the user, not to you. The fix is not a better check in the browser. The fix is that the server decides, and the browser only asks.
paywall.incident: Enrichlead was built entirely with an AI coding tool. Within 72 hours of launch, users bypassed the whole subscription from the console and maxed out the API keys. The founder shut the app down.

ten.heading: Ten ways an AI-built app leaks.
ten.subtitle: Every number here comes from a published scan or a documented incident. We did not make any of them up, and we will show you the source for each.
ten.t1: Your database is readable by strangers
ten.b1: 85% of scanned apps were missing row-level security on SELECT. The key that reads it is in your browser bundle. Nobody has to hack anything.
ten.t2: Your API keys are in the page
ten.b2: 62% had keys exposed in the client. About 4% shipped the Supabase service-role key, which is the one that ignores every rule you wrote.
ten.t3: Anyone can log in as anyone
ten.b3: 45% had an authentication bypass. Base44 shipped one where you could register into any private app using an ID printed in the URL.
ten.s3: VibeEval, and Wiz security research on Base44
ten.t4: Your paywall is a browser variable
ten.b4: 27% of monetized apps gated a paid feature in the client. A user changes one value in the console and he is on Pro.
ten.b5: 34% of apps using storage left a bucket open. The Tea app leaked 72,000 images including government photo IDs through exactly this.
ten.s5: VibeEval, and reported breach of the Tea app
ten.b6: Replit's agent wiped a live production database during an explicit code freeze, destroyed records for 1,206 executives, then told the founder rollback was impossible. It was not.
ten.s6: The Register and Fortune, on the SaaStr incident
ten.t7: The code fails a basic security test
ten.b7: 45% of AI-generated code fails OWASP Top 10 tests, across 100+ models and 80 tasks. 86% failed to defend against cross-site scripting. The models get better at working code and no better at secure code.
ten.t8: Your bill can be run up by anyone
ten.b8: No rate limits, no spend caps. A single abusive user calls your model endpoint in a loop and your card pays for it until you notice.
ten.s8: Enrichlead, founder's own account of the incident
ten.t9: The AI can no longer edit its own code
ten.b9: Duplicated logic across files with slight variations. You change one place and the other three stay broken. This is the wall people hit around the 200th prompt.
ten.s9: Observed in every rescue we have read about
ten.t10: There is no way to hand it over
ten.b10: No version control, no tests, no deployment story. Which means there is exactly one person who can safely touch it, and that person is you, forever.
ten.s10: The reason most people call us
ten.note: We are not going to quote the 8,000 startups and the 4 billion dollar cleanup market that circulate on this topic. Those trace to vendor blogs with no source, and using them would make everything else on this page worth less.

rls.heading: The server can say “200 OK” while handing strangers every customer.
rls.subtitle: Watch the same request twice. First the table has no row rules. Then we enable them and send it again.
rls.keyNote: This public browser key identifies the project. Row rules decide which records it may read.
rls.hint: Now enable row rules and send the same request.
rls.tableAria: Fictional customers returned by the demo request
rls.emptyRow: The request still succeeds, but no customer row is visible.
rls.verdictOpen: {n} customer rows crossed the browser without a login.
rls.verdictLocked: The same request returned 200 OK and an empty array.
rls.punch: An open database does not fail loudly. It answers.
rls.stat: In a published scan of 1,430+ Lovable apps, 85% were missing row-level security on SELECT.
rls.honest: A free outside scan can find the browser key, but it cannot verify the database rules inside. That check belongs in the full audit.

fix.eyebrow: Finding it is not fixing it
fix.heading: A key is repaired only when the old one is revoked and the replacement leaves the browser.
fix.subtitle: One complete repair: find the exposed key, revoke it, move its replacement server-side, then scan the public files again.
fix.redacted: The value is redacted and cannot be used.
fix.serverOnly: Replacement exists only on the server
fix.scanningText: Checking the public files a browser downloads…
fix.exposedText: A redacted key was found in the browser bundle.
fix.revokingText: Revoking the old key so it can no longer authorise a request…
fix.serverSideText: The replacement moved into the server environment and is no longer sent to the browser.
fix.rescanningText: Checking the same public files again…
fix.cleanText: The rescan found no key in the browser bundle.
fix.outcome: The repair is complete: the old key is revoked, the replacement is server-side, and the rescan is clean.
